1.1: The wordes of the Preacher, the sonne of David King in Jerusalem.
1.2: Vanitie of vanities, sayth the Preacher: vanitie of vanities, all is vanitie.
1.3: What remaineth unto man in all his travail, which he suffereth under ye sunne?
1.4: One generation passeth, and another generation succeedeth: but the earth remaineth for ever.
1.5: The sunne riseth, and ye sunne goeth down, and draweth to his place, where he riseth.
1.6: The wind goeth toward the South, and compasseth toward the North: the wind goeth round about, and returneth by his circuites.
1.7: All the rivers goe into the sea, yet the sea is not full: for the rivers goe unto ye place, whence they return, and goe.
1.8: All things are full of labour: man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
1.9: What is it that hath been? that that shalbe: and what is it that hath been done? that which shalbe done: and there is no new thing under the sunne.
1.10: Is there any thing, whereof one may say, Behold this, it is new? it hath been already in the old time that was before us.
1.11: There is no memorie of the former, neither shall there be a remembrance of the latter that shalbe, with them that shall come after.
1.12: I the Preacher have been King over Israel in Jerusalem:
1.13: And I have given mine heart to search and find out wisdom by all things that are done under the heaven: (this sore travail hath GOD given to the sonnes of men, to humble them thereby)
1.14: I have considered all the workes that are done under the sunne, and behold, all is vanitie, and vexation of the spirit.
1.15: That which is crooked, can none make straight: and that which faileth, cannot be nombred.
1.16: I thought in mine heart, and said, Behold, I am become great, and excel in wisdom all them that have been before me in Jerusalem: and mine heart hath seen much wisedome and knowledge.
1.17: And I gave mine heart to know wisdom and knowledge, madnes and foolishnes: I knew also that this is a vexation of the spirit.
1.18: For in the multitude of wisedome is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge, increaseth sorowe.

2.1: I said in mine heart, Goe to now, I will prove thee with joy: therefore take thou pleasure in pleasant things: and behold, this also is vanitie.
2.2: I said of laughter, Thou art mad: and of joy, What is this that thou doest?
2.3: I sought in mine heart to give my self to wine, and to lead mine heart in wisdom, and to take hold of follie, till I might see where is that goodness of the children of men, which they enioy under the sunne: the whole nomber of the dayes of their life.
2.4: I have made my great workes: I have built me houses: I have planted me vineyards.
2.5: I have made me gardens and orchards, and planted in them trees of all fruit.
2.6: I have made me cisternes of water, to water therewith the woods that grow with trees.
2.7: I have gotten servants and maides, and had children borne in the house: also I had great possession of beeves and sheep above all that were before me in Jerusalem.
2.8: I have gathered unto me also silver and gold, and the chief treasures of Kings and provinces: I have provided me men singers and women singers, and the delites of the sonnes of men, as a woman taken captive, and women taken captives.
2.9: And I was great, and increased above all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisedome remained with me.
2.10: And whatsoever mine eyes desired, I withheld it not from them: I withdrew not mine heart from any joy: for mine heart reioyced in al my labour: and this was my portion of all my travail.
2.11: Then I looked on all my workes that mine hands had wrought, and on the travail that I had laboured to doe: and behold, all is vanitie and vexation of the spirit: and there is no profit under the sunne.
2.12: And I turned to behold wisedome, and madnes and follie: (for who is the man that will come after the King in things, which men now have done?)
2.13: Then I saw that there is profit in wisdom, more then in follie: as the light is more excellent then darkenes.
2.14: For the wise mans eyes are in his head, but the fool walketh in darknes: yet I know also that the same condition falleth to them all.
2.15: Then I thought in mine heart, It befalleth unto me, as it befalleth to ye fool. Why therefore doe I then labour to be more wise? And I sayd in mine heart, that this also is vanitie.
2.16: For there shalbe no remembrance of the wise, nor of the fool for ever: for that that now is, in the dayes to come shall all be forgotten. And how dyeth the wise man, as doeth the fool?
2.17: Therefore I hated life: for the work that is wrought under the sunne is grieuous unto me: for all is vanitie, and vexation of the spirit.
2.18: I hated also all my labour, wherein I had travailed under the sunne, which I shall leave to the man that shalbe after me.
2.19: And who knoweth whether he shalbe wise or foolish? yet shall hee have rule over all my labour, wherein I have travailed, and wherein I have shewed my self wise under the sunne. This is also vanitie.
2.20: Therefore I went about to make mine heart abhorre all the labour, wherein I had travailed under the sunne.
2.21: For there is a man whose travail is in wisdom, and in knowledge and in equitie: yet to a man that hath not travailed herein, shall he give his portion: this also is vanitie and a great grief.
2.22: For what hath man of all his travail and grief of his heart, wherein he hath travailed under the sunne?
2.23: For all his dayes are sorowes, and his travail grief: his heart also taketh not rest in the night: which also is vanitie.
2.24: There is no profit to man: but that he eat, and drink, and delight his soul with the profit of his labour: I saw also this, that it was of the hand of God.
2.25: For who could eat, and who could haste to outward things more then I?
2.26: Surely to a man that is good in his sight, God giveth wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he giveth pain, to gather, and to heap to give to him that is good before God: this is also vanitie, and vexation of the spirit.

3.1: To all things there is an appointed time, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
3.2: A time to bee borne, and a time to die: a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted.
3.3: A time to slay, and a time to heal: a time to break down, and a time to build.
3.4: A time to weep, and a time to laugh: a time to mourn, and a time to dance.
3.5: A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones: a time to embrace, and a time to be far from embracing.
3.6: A time to seek, and a time to lose: a time to keep, and a time to cast away.
3.7: A time to rent, and a time to sow: a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
3.8: A time to love, and a time to hate: a time of war, and a time of peace.
3.9: What profit hath hee that worketh of the thing wherein he travaileth?
3.10: I have seen the travail that God hath given to ye sonnes of men to humble them thereby.
3.11: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, yet can not man find out the work that God hath wrought from the beginning even to the end.
3.12: I know that there is nothing good in them, but to reioyce, and to doe good in his life.
3.13: And also that every man eateth and drinketh, and seeth the commoditie of all his labour. this is the gift of God.
3.14: I know that whatsoever God shall doe, it shalbe for ever: to it can no man add, and from it can none diminish: for God hath done it, that they should fear before him.
3.15: What is that that hath been? that is now: and that that shalbe, hath now been: for God requireth that which is past.
3.16: And moreover I have seen under the sunne the place of iudgement, where was wickedness, and the place of justice where was iniquitie.
3.17: I thought in mine heart, God wil judge the just and the wicked: for time is there for every purpose and for every work.
3.18: I considered in mine heart the state of the children of men that God had purged them: yet to see to, they are in themselves as beastes.
3.19: For the condition of the children of men, and the condition of beasts are even as one condition unto them. As the one dyeth, so dyeth the other: for they have all one breath, and there is no excellency of man above ye beast: for all is vanitie.
3.20: All goe to one place, and all was of the dust, and all shall return to the dust.
3.21: Who knoweth whether the spirit of man ascend upward, and the spirit of the beast descend downeward to the earth?
3.22: Therefore I see that there is nothing better then that a man should reioyce in his affaires, because that is his portion. For who shall bring him to see what shalbe after him?

4.1: So I turned and considered all the oppressions that are wrought under the sunne, and behold the teares of the oppressed, and none comforteth them: and lo, the strength is of the hand of them that oppress them, and none comforteth them.
4.2: Wherefore I praysed the dead which now are dead, above the living, which are yet alive.
4.3: And I count him better then them both, which hath not yet bin: for he hath not seen the evil workes which are wrought under the sunne.
4.4: Also I beheld all travail, and all perfection of workes that this is ye enuie of a man against his neighbour: this also is vanitie and vexation of spirit.
4.5: The fool foldeth his hands, and eateth up his own flesh.
4.6: Better is an handful with quietness, then two handfuls with labour and vexation of spirit.
4.7: Again I returned, and saw vanitie under the sunne.
4.8: There is one alone, and there is not a second, which hath neither sonne nor brother, yet is there none end of all his travail, neither can his eye be satisfied with riches: neither doeth he think, For whom doe I travail and defraud my soul of pleasure? this also is vanitie, and this is an evil travail.
4.9: Two are better then one: for they have better wages for their labour.
4.10: For if they fal, the one wil lift up his felow: but wo unto him that is alone: for he falleth, and there is not a second to lift him up.
4.11: Also if two sleep together, then shall they have heat: but to one how should there be heat?
4.12: And if one overcome him, two shall stand against him: and a threefold coard is not easily broken.
4.13: Better is a poor and wise child, then an old and foolish King, which will no more be admonished.
4.14: For out of the prison he cometh forth to reign: when as he that is borne in his kingdom, is made poor.
4.15: I beheld all the living, which walk under the sunne, with the second child, which shall stand up in his place.
4.16: There is none end of all the people, nor of all that were before them, and they that come after, shall not reioyce in him: surely this is also vanitie and vexation of spirit.
4.17: Take heed to thy foot when thou entrest into the House of God, and be more neere to hear then to give the sacrifice of fooles: for they know not that they doe evil.

5.1: Be not rash with thy mouth, nor let thine heart be hastie to utter a thing before God: for God is in the heavens, and thou art on the earth: therefore let thy wordes be few.
5.2: For as a dream cometh by the multitude of business: so the voyce of a fool is in the multitude of wordes.
5.3: When thou hast vowed a vow to God, deferre not to pay it: for he deliteth not in fooles: pay therefore that thou hast vowed.
5.4: It is better that thou shouldest not vow, then that thou shouldest vow and not pay it.
5.5: Suffer not thy mouth to make thy flesh to sinne: neither say before the Angel, that this is ignorance: wherefore shall God bee angry by thy voyce, and destroy the work of thine hands?
5.6: For in the multitude of dreames, and vanities are also many wordes: but fear thou God.
5.7: If in a countrey thou seest the oppression of the poor, and the defrauding of iudgement and justice, be not astonied at the matter: for hee that is higher then the highest, regardeth, and there be higher then they.
5.8: And the abundance of the earth is over all: the King also consisteth by the field that is tilled.
5.9: He that loveth silver, shall not be satisfied with silver, and he that loveth riches, shalbe without the fruit thereof: this also is vanitie.
5.10: When goods increase, they are increased that eat them: and what good cometh to the owners thereof, but the beholding thereof with their eyes?
5.11: The sleep of him that traueileth, is sweet, whether he eat litle or much: but the sacietie of the rich will not suffer him to sleep.
5.12: There is an evil sickenes that I have seen under the sunne: to wit, riches reserved to the owners thereof for their evil.
5.13: And these riches perish by evil travel, and he begetteth a sonne, and in his hand is nothing.
5.14: As hee came foorth of his mothers belly, he shall return naked to goe as he came, and shall bear away nothing of his labour, which hee hath caused to pass by his hand.
5.15: And this also is an evil sickenes that in all pointes as he came, so shall he goe, and what profit hath he that he hath traueiled for the wind?
5.16: Also all his dayes hee eateth in darkenes with much grief, and in his sorowe and anger.
5.17: Behold then, what I have seen good, that it is comely to eat, and to drink, and to take pleasure in all his labour, wherein he traueileth under the sunne, the whole nomber of the dayes of his life, which God giveth him: for this is his portion.
5.18: Also to every man to whom God hath given riches and treasures, and giveth him power to eat thereof, and to take his part, and to enioy his labour: this is the gift of God.
5.19: Surely hee will not much remember the dayes of his life, because God answereth to the joy of his heart.

6.1: There is an evil, which I saw under the sunne, and it is much among men:
6.2: A man to whom God hath given riches and treasures and honour, and he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that it desireth: but God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a strange man shall eat it up: this is vanitie, and this is an evil sickness.
6.3: If a man beget an hundreth children and live many yeeres, and the dayes of his yeeres be multiplied, and his soul be not satisfied with good things, and he be not buried, I say that an untimely fruit is better then he.
6.4: For he cometh into vanitie and goeth into darkenesse: and his name shall be covered with darkenesse.
6.5: Also he hath not seen ye sunne, nor knowen it: therefore this hath more rest then the other.
6.6: And if he had lived a thousand yeeres twise told, and had seen no good, shall not all goe to one place?
6.7: All the labour of man is for his mouth: yet the soul is not filled.
6.8: For what hath the wise man more then the fool? what hath the poor that knoweth how to walk before the living?
6.9: The sight of ye eye is better then to walk in ye lustes: this also is vanitie, and vexation of spirit.
6.10: What is that that hath been? the name thereof is now named: and it is knowen that it is man: and he cannot strive with him that is stronger then he.

7.1: Surely there be many things that increase vanitie: and what availeth it man?
7.2: For who knoweth what is good for man in the life and in the nomber of the dayes of the life of his vanitie, seeing he maketh them as a shadow? For who can shew unto man what shall be after him under the sunne?
7.3: A good name is better then a good oyntment, and the day of death, then the day that one is borne.
7.4: It is better to goe to the house of mourning, then to goe to the house of feasting, because this is the end of all men: and the living shall lay it to his heart.
7.5: Anger is better then laughter: for by a sad look the heart is made better.
7.6: The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning: but the heart of fooles is in the house of mirth.
7.7: Better it is to hear ye rebuke of a wise man, then that a man should hear the song of fooles.
7.8: For like ye noyse of the thornes under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool: this also is vanitie.
7.9: Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad: and the reward destroyeth the heart.
7.10: The end of a thing is better then the beginning thereof, and the pacient in spirit is better then the proud in spirit.
7.11: Be not thou of an hastie spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fooles.
7.12: Say not thou, Why is it that the former dayes were better then these? for thou doest not enquire wisely of this thing.
7.13: Wisedome is good with an inheritance, and excellent to them that see the sunne.
7.14: For man shall rest in the shadow of wisedome, and in the shadow of silver: but the excellencie of the knowledge of wisedome giveth life to the possessers thereof.
7.15: Behold the work of God: for who can make straight that which he hath made crooked?
7.16: In the day of wealth be of good comfort, and in the day of affliction consider: God also hath made this contrary to that, to the intent that man should find nothing after him.
7.17: I have seen all things in the dayes of my vanitie: there is a just man that perisheth in his justice, and there is a wicked man that continueth long in his malice.
7.18: Be not thou just ouermuch, neither make thy self ouerwise: wherefore shouldest thou be desolate?
7.19: Be not thou wicked ouermuch, neither be thou foolish: wherefore shouldest thou perish not in thy time?
7.20: It is good that thou lay hold on this: but yet withdraw not thine hand from that: for he that feareth God, shall come forth of them all.
7.21: Wisedome shall strengthen the wise man more then ten mightie princes that are in ye citie.
7.22: Surely there is no man just in the earth, that doeth good and sinneth not.
7.23: Give not thine heart also to all ye wordes that men speak, lest thou doe hear thy servant cursing thee.
7.24: For often times also thine heart knoweth that thou likewise hast cursed others.
7.25: All this have I prooued by wisedome: I thought I will be wise, but it went far from me.
7.26: It is far off, what may it be? and it is a profound deepenesse, who can find it?
7.27: I have compassed about, both I and mine heart to know and to enquire and to search wisedome, and reason, and to know the wickedness of follie, and the foolishness of madness,
7.28: And I find more bitter then death the woman whose heart is as nettes and snares, and her handes, as bands: he that is good before God, shalbe delivered from her, but the sinner shall be taken by her.
7.29: Behold, sayth the Preacher, this have I found, seeking one by one to find the count:
7.30: And yet my soul seeketh, but I find it not: I have found one man of a thousand: but a woman among them all have I not found.
7.31: Onely loe, this have I found, that God hath made man righteous: but they have sought many inventions.

8.1: Who is as the wise man? and who knoweth the interpretation of a thing? the wisedome of a man doth make his face to shine: and the strength of his face shalbe changed.
8.2: I advertise thee to take heed to ye mouth of the King, and to the word of the othe of God.
8.3: Haste not to goe forth of his sight: stand not in an evil thing: for he will doe whatsoever pleaseth him.
8.4: Where the word of ye King is, there is power, and who shall say unto him, What doest thou?
8.5: He that keepeth the commandement, shall know none evil thing, and the heart of the wise shall know the time and iudgement.
8.6: For to every purpose there is a time and iudgement, because the miserie of man is great upon him.
8.7: For he knoweth not that which shalbe: for who can tell him when it shalbe?
8.8: Man is not lord over the spirit to retain the spirit: neither hath hee power in the day of death, nor deliverance in the battell, neither shall wickedness deliver the possessers thereof.
8.9: All this have I seen, and have given mine heart to every work, which is wrought under the sunne, and I saw a time that man ruleth over man to his own hurt.
8.10: And likewise I saw the wicked buried, and they returned, and they that came from the holy place, were yet forgotten in the citie where they had done right: this also is vanitie.
8.11: Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the children of men is fully set in them to doe evil.
8.12: Though a sinner doe evil an hundreth times, and God prolongeth his dayes, yet I know that it shalbe well with them that fear the Lord, and doe reverence before him.
8.13: But it shall not be well to the wicked, neither shall he prolong his dayes: he shall be like a shadow, because he feareth not before God.
8.14: There is a vanitie, which is done upon the earth, that there be righteous men to whom it cometh according to the work of the wicked: and there be wicked men to whom it cometh according to the work of the just: I thought also that this is vanitie.
8.15: And I praysed joy: for there is no goodness to man under the sunne, save to eat and to drink and to reioyce: for this is adioyned to his labour, the dayes of his life that God hath given him under the sunne.
8.16: When I applied mine heart to know wisedome, and to behold the busines that is done on earth, that neither day nor night the eyes of man take sleep,
8.17: Then I beheld the whole work of God, that man cannot find out ye work that is wrought under the sunne: for the which man laboureth to seek it, and cannot find it: yea, and though the wise man think to know it, he cannot find it.

9.1: I have surely given mine heart to all this, and to declare all this, that the just, and the wise, and their workes are in the hand of God: and no man knoweth eyther love or hatred of all that is before them.
9.2: All things come alike to all: and the same condition is to the just and to the wicked, to the good and to the pure, and to the polluted, and to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as is the good, so is the sinner, he that sweareth, as he that feareth an othe.
9.3: This is evil among all that is done under the sunne, that there is one condition to all, and also the heart of the sonnes of men is full of evil, and madnes is in their heartes whiles they live, and after that, they goe to the dead.
9.4: Surely whosoever is ioyned to all ye living, there is hope: for it is better to a living dog, then to a dead lyon.
9.5: For the living know that they shall dye, but the dead know nothing at all: neither have they any more a reward: for their remembrance is forgotten.
9.6: Also their love, and their hatred, and their enuie is now perished, and they have no more portion for ever, in all that is done under the sunne.
9.7: Goe, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a cheerefull heart: for God now accepteth thy workes.
9.8: At all times let thy garments be white, and let not oyle be lacking upon thine head.
9.9: Reioyce with the wife whom thou hast loved all the dayes of the life of thy vanitie, which God hath given thee under the sunne all the dayes of thy vanitie: for this is thy portion in the life, and in thy travail wherein thou labourest under the sunne.
9.10: All that thine hand shall find to doe, doe it with all thy power: for there is neither work nor inuention, nor knowledge, nor wisedome in the grave whither thou goest.
9.11: I returned, and I saw under the sunne that the race is not to the swift, nor the battell to the strong, nor yet bread to the wise, nor also riches to men of understanding, neither yet fauour to men of knowledge: but time and chance cometh to them all.
9.12: For neither doth man know his time, but as the fishes which are taken in an evil net, and as the birdes that are caught in the snare: so are the children of men snared in the evil time when it falleth upon them suddenly.
9.13: I have also seen this wisedome under the sunne, and it is great unto me.
9.14: A litle citie and few men in it, and a great King came against it, and compassed it about, and builded fortes against it.
9.15: And there was found therein a poor and wise man, and he delivered the citie by his wisedome: but none remembred this poor man.
9.16: Then said I, Better is wisdom then strength: yet the wisedome of the poor is despised, and his wordes are not heard.
9.17: The wordes of the wise are more heard in quietnes, then the cry of him that ruleth among fooles.
9.18: Better is wisedome then weapons of war: but one sinner destroyeth much good.

10.1: Dead flies cause to stink, and putrifie the ointment of the apoticarie: so doeth a litle follie him that is in estimation for wisedome, and for glorie.
10.2: The heart of a wise man is at his right hand: but the heart of a fool is at his left hand.
10.3: And also when the fool goeth by the way, his heart faileth, and he telleth unto all that he is a fool.
10.4: If the spirit of him that ruleth, rise up against thee, leave not thy place: for gentlenes pacifieth great sinnes.
10.5: There is an evil that I have seen under the sunne, as an errour that proceedeth from the face of him that ruleth.
10.6: Follie is set in great excellencie, and the rich set in the low place.
10.7: I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking as servants on the ground.
10.8: He that diggeth a pit, shall fal into it, and he that breaketh the hedge, a serpent shall bite him.
10.9: He that remooueth stones, shall hurt himself thereby, and hee that cutteth wood, shall be in danger thereby.
10.10: If the yron be blunt, and one hath not whet the edge, he must then put to more strength: but the excellencie to direct a thing is wisedome.
10.11: If the serpent bite, when he is not charmed: no better is a babbler.
10.12: The words of ye mouth of a wise man have grace: but the lippes of a fool deuoure himself.
10.13: The beginning of the wordes of his mouth is foolishness, and the latter end of his mouth is wicked madness.
10.14: For the fool multiplieth woordes, saying, Man knoweth not what shall be: and who can tell him what shall be after him?
10.15: The labour of the foolish doeth wearie him: for he knoweth not to goe into the citie.
10.16: Woe to thee, O land, when thy King is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning.
10.17: Blessed art thou, O land, when thy King is the sonne of nobles, and thy princes eat in time, for strength and not for drunkenness.
10.18: By slouthfulnes the roof of the house goeth to decaie, and by the ydlenesse of the handes the house droppeth through.
10.19: They prepare bread for laughter, and wine comforteth the living, but silver answereth to all.
10.20: Curse not the King, no not in thy thought, neither curse the rich in thy bed chamber: for the fowl of the heaven shall carie the voice, and that which hath wings, shall declare the matter.

11.1: Cast thy bread upon the waters: for after many daies thou shalt find it.
11.2: Give a portion to seven, and also to eight: for thou knowest not what evil shalbe upon ye earth.
11.3: If the clouds be full, they wil powre forth rain upon the earth: and if the tree doe fall toward the South, or toward the North, in the place that the tree falleth, there it shalbe.
11.4: He that observeth ye wind, shall not sow, and he that regardeth the cloudes, shall not reap.
11.5: As thou knowest not which is ye way of the spirit, nor how the bones doe grow in the womb of her that is with child: so thou knowest not the work of God that worketh all.
11.6: In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening let not thine hand rest: for thou knowest not whither shall prosper, this or that, or whether both shalbe a like good.
11.7: Surely the light is a pleasant thing: and it is a good thing to the eyes to see the sunne.
11.8: Though a man live many yeeres, and in them all he reioyce, yet hee shall remember the daies of darkenesse, because they are manie, all that cometh is vanitie.
11.9: Reioyce, O yong man, in thy youth, and let thine heart cheer thee in the dayes of thy youth: and walk in the waies of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know that for all these things, God wil bring thee to iudgement.
11.10: Therefore take away grief out of thine heart, and cause evil to depart from thy flesh: for childehood and youth are vanitie.

12.1: Remember now thy Creator in the daies of thy youth, whiles the evil daies come not, nor the yeeres approche, wherein thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them:
12.2: Whiles the sunne is not dark, nor ye light, nor the moon, nor the starres, nor the cloudes return after the rain:
12.3: When the keepers of ye house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow them selves, and the grinders shall cease, because they are few, and they wax dark that look out by ye windowes:
12.4: And the doores shall be shut without by the base sound of the grinding, and he shall rise up at the voice of the bird: and all the daughters of singing shall be abased.
12.5: Also they shalbe afraid of the hie thing, and fear shalbe in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grassehopper shall be a burden, and concupiscence shall be driven away: for man goeth to the house of his age, and the mourners goe about in the street.
12.6: Whiles the silver coarde is not lengthened, nor the golden ewer broken, nor the pitcher broken at the well, nor the wheel broken at the cistern:
12.7: And dust return to the earth as it was, and the spirit return to God that gave it.
12.8: Vanitie of vanities, saieth the Preacher, all is vanitie.
12.9: And the more wise the Preacher was, the more he taught the people knowledge, and caused them to hear, and searched foorth, and prepared many parables.
12.10: The Preacher sought to find out pleasant wordes, and an upright writing, even the wordes of trueth.
12.11: The wordes of the wise are like goads, and like nailes fastened by the masters of the assemblies, which are given by one pastour.
12.12: And of other things beside these, my son, take thou heed: for there is none end in making many bookes, and much reading is a wearines of the flesh.
12.13: Let us hear the end of all: fear God and keep his commandements: for this is the whole duetie of man.
12.14: For God will bring every work unto iudgement, with every secret thing, whether it be good or evil.

21:1:1: Solomon is here called a preacher, or one that assembleth the people, because he teacheth the true knowledge of God, and how men ought to pass their life in this transitory world.
21:1:2: He condemneth the opinions of all men that set felicity in any thing, but in God alone, seeing that in this world all things are as vanity and nothing.
21:1:3: Solomon doth not condemn man’s labor or diligence, but showeth that there is no full contentation in any thing under the heaven, nor in any creature, forasmuch as all things are transitory.
21:1:4: One man dieth after another, and the earth remaineth longest, even to the last day, which yet is subject to corruption.
21:1:6: By the sun, wind and rivers, he showeth that the greatest labor and longest hath an end, and therefore there can be no felicity in this world.
21:1:7: The sea which compasseth all the earth, filleth the veins thereof, the which pour out springs and rivers into the sea again.
21:1:9: He speaketh of times and seasons, and things done in them, which as they have been in times past, so come they to pass again.
21:1:12: He proveth that if any could have attained to felicity in this world by labor, and study, he chiefly should have obtained it, because he had gifts and aids of God thereunto above all others.
21:1:13: Man of nature hath a desire to know, and yet is not able to come to the perfection of knowledge, which is the punishment of sin, to humble man, and to teach him to depend only upon God.
21:1:15: Man is not able by all his diligence to cause things to go otherwise than they do: neither can he number the faults that are committed, much less remedy them.
21:1:17: That is, vain things, which served unto pleasure, wherein was no commodity, but grief and trouble of conscience.
21:1:18: Wisdom and knowledge cannot be come by without great pain of body and mind: for when a man hath attained to the highest, yet is his mind never fully content: therefore in this world is no true felicity.
21:2:1: Solomon maketh this discourse with himself, as though he would try whether there were contentation in ease and pleasures.
21:2:3: Hebrew, draw my flesh to wine.
Albeit I gave myself to pleasures, yet I thought to keep wisdom and the fear of God in mine heart, and govern mine affairs by the same.
21:2:7: Meaning, of the servants or slaves, which he had bought: so the children born in their servitude, were the masters.
21:2:8: That is, whatsoever men take pleasure in.
Which were the most beautiful of them that were taken in war, as Judg. 5:30. Some understand by these words, no women, but instruments of music.
21:2:9: For all this God did not take his gift of wisdom from me.
21:2:10: This was the fruit of all my labor, a certain pleasure mixed with care, which he calleth vanity in the next verse.
21:2:12: I bethought with myself whether it were better to follow wisdom, or mine own affections and pleasures, which he calleth madness.
21:2:14: He forseeth things, which the fool cannot for lack of wisdom.
For both die and are forgotten as verse 16, or they both alike have prosperity or adversity.
21:2:16: He wondereth that men forget a wise man, being dead, as soon as they do a fool.
21:2:20: That I might seek the true felicity which is in God.
21:2:21: Among other griefs that was not the least, to leave that which he had gotten by great travail, to one that had taken no pain therefore, and whom he knew not whether he were a wise man or a fool.
21:2:24: When man hath all labored, he can get no more than food and refreshing, yet he confesseth also that this cometh of God’s blessing, as Eccl. 3:13.
21:3:1: He speaketh of this diversity of time for two causes: first to declare that there is nothing in this world perpetual: next to teach us not to be grieved, if we have not all things at once according to our desires, neither enjoy them so long as we would wish.
21:3:11: God hath given man a desire, and affection to seek out the things of this world, and to labor therein.
21:3:13: Read Eccl. 2:24, and these places declare that we should do all things with sobriety and in the fear of God, forasmuch as he giveth not his gifts to the intent that they should be abused.
21:3:14: That is, man shall never be able to let God’s work, but as he hath determined, so it shall come to pass.
21:3:15: God only causeth that, which is past, to return.
21:3:17: Meaning, with God, howsoever man neglect his duty.
21:3:18: And made them pure in their first creation.
21:3:19: Man is not able by his reason and judgment to put difference between man and beast, as touching those things whereunto both are subject: for the eye cannot judge any otherwise of a man being dead, than of a beast, which is dead: yet by the word of God and faith we easily know the diversity, as verse 21.
21:3:21: Meaning, that reason cannot comprehend that which faith believeth herein.
21:3:22: By the often repetition of this sentence, as Eccl. 2:24; 3:12, 22; 5:17 and 8:15, he declareth that man by reason can comprehend nothing better in this life, than to use the gifts of God soberly and comfortably: for to know further, is a special gift of God revealed by his Spirit.
21:4:1: He maketh here another discourse with himself concerning the tyranny of them that oppressed the poor.
21:4:2: Because they are no more subject to these oppressions.
21:4:3: He speaketh according to the judgment of the flesh, which cannot abide to feel or see troubles.
21:4:4: The more perfect that the work is, the more it is envied of the wicked.
21:4:5: For idleness he is compelled to destroy himself.
21:4:9: Forasmuch as when man is alone, he can neither help himself nor others, he showeth that men ought to live in mutual society to the intent they may be profitable one to another, and that their things may increase.
21:4:12: By this proverb he declareth how necessary it is, that men should live in society.
21:4:14: That is, from a poor and base estate, or out of trouble and prison, as Joseph did, Gen. 41:14.
Meaning, that is born a King.
21:4:15: Which follow and flatter the King’s son, or him that shall succeed, to enter into credit with them in hope of gain.
21:4:16: They never cease by all means to creep into favor, but when they obtain not, their greedy desires, they think themselves abused, as others have been in time past, and so care no more for him.
21:4:17: That is, with what affection thou comest to hear the word of God.
Meaning, of the wicked, which think to please God with common uses, and have neither faith nor repentance.
21:5:1: He heareth thee not for thy many words’ sake, or often repetitions, but considereth thy faith and servant mind.
Either in vowing or in praying: meaning, that we should use all reverence to Godward.
21:5:3: He speaketh of vows, which are approved by God’s word, and serve to his glory.
21:5:5: That is, before God’s messenger, when he shall examine thy doing, as though thy ignorance should be a just excuse.
Cause not thyself to sin by vowing rashly: as they do which make a vow to live unmarried, and such like.
21:5:7: Meaning, that God will redress these things, and therefore we must depend upon him.
21:5:8: The earth is to be preferred above all things which appertain to this life.
Kings and Princes cannot maintain their estate without tillage, which thing commendeth the excellency of tillage.
21:5:11: That is, his great abundance of riches, or the surfeiting, which cometh by his great feeding.
21:5:12: When covetous men heap up riches, which turn to their destruction.
21:5:13: He doth not enjoy his father’s riches.
21:5:15: Meaning, in vain, and without profit.
21:5:16: In affliction and grief of mind.
21:5:19: He will take no great thought for the pains that he hath endured in time past.
21:6:2: He showeth that it is the plague of God when the rich man hath not a liberal heart to use his riches.
21:6:3: If he can never have enough.

As we see oftentimes that the covetous man either falleth into crimes that deserve death, or is murdered or drowned or hangeth himself, or such like, and so lacketh the honor of burial, which is the last office of humanity.
21:6:4: Meaning, the untimely fruit whose life did neither profit or hurt any.
21:6:8: That knoweth to use his goods well in the judgment of men.
21:6:9: To be content with that which God hath given, is better than to follow the desires that never can be satisfied.
21:6:10: Meaning, God who will make him to feel that he is mortal.
21:7:2: There is no state wherein man can live to have perfect quietness in this life.
21:7:3: He speaketh thus after the judgment of the flesh, which thinketh death to be the end of all evils, or else, because that this corporal death is the entering into life everlasting.
21:7:4: Where we may see the hand of God, and learn to examine our lives.
21:7:8: Which crackle for a while and profit nothing.
21:7:9: A man that is esteemed wise, when he falleth to oppression, becometh like a beast.
21:7:10: He noteth their lightness which enterprise a thing and suddenly leave it off again.
21:7:12: Murmur not against God when he sendeth adversities for man’s sins.
21:7:13: He answereth to them that esteem not wisdom except riches be joined therewith, showing that both are the gifts of God, but that wisdom is far more excellent, and may be without riches.
21:7:16: Consider wherefore God doth send it and what may comfort thee.
That man should be able to control nothing in his works.
21:7:17: Meaning, that cruel tyrants put the godly to death and let the wicked go free.
21:7:18: Boast not too much of thine own justice and wisdom.
21:7:19: Tarry not long when thou art admonished to come out of the way of wickedness.
21:7:20: Consider what desolation and destruction shall come, if thou do not obey them.
To wit, on these admonitions that go before.
21:7:23: Credit them not, neither care for them.
21:7:29: That is, to come to a conclusion.
21:7:31: And so are cause of their own destruction.
21:8:1: That is, doth get him favor and prosperity.
Whereas before he was proud and arrogant, he shall become humble and meek.
21:8:2: That is, that thou obey the king and keep the oath that thou hast made for the same cause.
21:8:3: Withdraw not thyself lightly from the obedience of thy prince.
21:8:5: That is, when time is to obey, and how far he should obey.
21:8:6: Man of himself is miserable, and therefore ought to do nothing to increase the same, but to work all things by wisdom and counsel.
21:8:8: Man hath no power to save his own life, and therefore must not rashly cast himself into danger.
21:8:9: As cometh ofttimes to tyrants and wicked rulers.
21:8:10: That is, others as wicked as they.
They that feared God and worshipped him according as he had appointed.
21:8:11: Where justice is delayed, there sin reigneth.
21:8:14: Which are punished as though they were wicked, as Eccl. 7:17.
21:9:1: Meaning, what things he ought to choose or refuse: or man knoweth not by these outward things, that is, by prosperity or adversity, whom God doth favor or hate, for he sendeth them as well to the wicked as to the godly.
21:9:3: In outward things, as riches and poverty, sickness and health, there is no difference between the godly and the wicked: but the difference is that the godly are assured by faith of God’s favor and assistance.
21:9:4: He noteth the Epicureans and carnal men, which made their belly their god, and had no pleasure, but in this life, wishing rather to be an abased and vile person in this life, than a man of authority, and so to die, which is meant by the dog and lion.
21:9:7: They flatter themselves to be in God’s favor, because they have all things in abundance.
21:9:8: Rejoice, be merry, and spare for no cost, thus speak the wicked belly-gods.
21:9:11: Thus the worldlings say to prove that all things are lawful for them, and attribute that to chance and fortune, which is done by the providence of God.
21:9:12: That is, he doth not foresee what shall come.
21:10:2: So that he doeth all things well and justly, where as the fool doeth the contrary.
21:10:3: By his doings he betrayeth himself.
21:10:4: If thy superior be angry with thee, be thou discrete, and not moved.
21:10:5: Meaning, that it is an evil thing when they that are in authority, fail and do not their duty.
21:10:6: They that are rich in wisdom and virtue.
21:10:10: Without wisdom whatsoever a man taketh in hand, turneth to his own hurt.
21:10:15: The ignorance and beastliness of the wicked is such that they know not common things, and yet will they discuss high matters.
21:10:16: Are given to their lusts, and pleasures.
That is, without wisdom and counsel.
21:10:17: Meaning, when he is noble for virtue and wisdom, and with the gifts of God.
21:10:20: Thou canst not work evil so secretly, but it shall be known.
21:11:1: That is, be liberal to the poor, and though it seem to be as a thing ventured on the sea, yet it shall bring thee profit.
21:11:3: As the clouds that are full, pour out rain, so the rich that have abundance, must distribute it liberally.
He exhorteth to be liberal while we live: for after, there is no power.
21:11:4: He that feareth inconveniences, when necessity requireth, shall never do his duty.
21:11:6: Be not weary of well doing.
That is, which of thy works are most agreeable to God.
21:11:8: That is, of affliction and trouble.
21:11:9: He derideth them that set their delight in worldly pleasures, as though God would not call count.
21:11:10: Meaning, carnal lusts, whereunto youth is given.
21:12:2: Before thou come to a continual misery: for when the clouds remain after the rain, man’s grief is increased.
21:12:3: The hands, which keep the body.
21:12:4: When the jaws, shall scarce open, and not be able to chew anymore.
That is, the wind pipes, or the ears shall be deaf and not able to hear singing.
He shall not be able to sleep.
21:12:5: They shall tremble as they go, as though they were afraid.
They shall be able to bear nothing.
To climb high because of their weakness, or they stoop down, as though they were afraid, lest anything should hit them.
Their head shall be as white as the blossoms of an almond tree.
21:12:6: That is, the heart, out of which the head draweth the powers of life.
Meaning, the marrow of the backbone and the sinews.
The little skin that covereth the brain, which is in color like gold.
21:12:7: The soul incontinently goeth either to joy or torment, and sleepeth not as the wicked imagine.
21:12:11: Which are well applied by the ministers, whom he calleth masters.
21:12:12: These things cannot be comprehended in books or learned by study, but God must instruct thine heart that thou mayest only know that wisdom is the true felicity, and the way thereunto is to fear God.
